query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Local variations in thermal expansion—resulting from retained microstructural heterogeneity—create residual stresses that, in turn, modify dislocation behavior and phase boundary dynamics, thereby unifying the observed stress–strain and thermoelastic responses (including tensile creep, microhardness changes, elastic modulus variation, and aging-induced hardening) in HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with natural microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Apply two distinct post-processing heat treatments: one that homogenizes the microstructure (minimizing local CTE differences) and one that preserves or accentuates the microstructural heterogeneity (enhancing local CTE mismatch), while keeping all other processing variables constant.
generation.conditions: Conduct mechanical tests over a broad temperature range—from ambient (≈293 K) up to high temperatures (≈1250 °C) for tensile creep, and specifically examine aging effects in the 600–800 °C range.
generation.structural_mediator: Residual stresses induced by local variations in the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) and the associated dislocation structures at heterogeneous phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During cooling (or subsequent thermal cycling), areas with different CTE values expand or contract at different rates. The resulting mismatch leads to internal residual stresses that influence dislocation movement and phase transformation behavior. This mechanism can simultaneously account for accelerated tensile creep at 1250 °C, changes in microhardness from cold rolling (due to altered dislocation densities), variations in elastic moduli across 293–1100 K, and hardening behavior after aging at intermediate temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogenized sample, the heterogeneous sample will exhibit (1) higher residual stress levels, (2) a higher rate of tensile creep at 1250 °C, (3) greater microhardness increase after cold deformation, and (4) altered elastic modulus trends over a wide temperature range. Aging at 600–800 °C should further amplify these differences by promoting local strain-induced transformations.
generation.baseline: The homogenized (post-heat treated to minimize microstructural and CTE variability) sample serves as the baseline, expected to show lower residual stresses and less pronounced anomalies in mechanical and thermoelastic properties.
generation.boundary: The predicted mechanism is most active in the high-temperature regime (near 1250 °C for tensile creep and 600–800 °C for aging-induced hardening) as well as during measurements of thermoelastic responses from 293 to 1100 K. Outside these bounds, the effects may be less pronounced or overshadowed by other mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of residual stress differences and their quantitative impact on mechanical properties remain uncertain. Additionally, potential competing mechanisms—for instance, those related to dislocation density alone—may also contribute, requiring careful isolation in the experimental design.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples that are identical except for their post-processing heat treatments: one set undergoes a homogenizing heat treatment to minimize microstructural heterogeneity and CTE differences, and the other is treated to preserve or accentuate heterogeneity. Measure tensile creep at 1250 °C, nanoindentation hardness, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and residual stress (e.g., via XRD) for each set.
measurements: Elastic modulus as a function of temperature (293–1100 K)
Residual stress distribution (using XRD or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically and thermoelastically measured properties (creep rate, hardness, elastic moduli, and residual stress levels) of the homogenized samples are statistically indistinguishable from those of the heterogeneous samples, then the hypothesis that local CTE mismatch-induced residual stresses drive the unified behavior would be falsified.

According to the figure, the thermal expansion coefficient of the alloy at 900–1100 K varies between 23 × 10−6 and 25 × 10−6, which is higher than that of austenitic stainless steel (16 × 10−6–17 × 10−6 K−1) in the same temperature range. Hence, the welded joints of the alloy will result in greater tensile stresses during solidification, and they are more susceptible to thermal cracking. Meanwhile, compared to the stainless steel plate, the aluminum alloy base plate has higher thermal conductivity. This indicates that the heat dissipation is more rapid and the weld cooling rate is faster, leading to a larger tensile strain rate.
